researcher_responses.full_research_review:
Audit completed

The 16-page clinical and regulatory review separates direct lipedema evidence from evidence transferred from heart failure, CKD, cirrhosis, hypertension, venous disease, lymphatic disease and idiopathic/orthostatic edema. It includes all requested drug classes, Spanish/EMA regulatory information, withdrawal evidence, monitoring and red flags, conflicts of interest, inaccessible-source notes, a registry audit, publication-safe Spanish wording and a falsation section.

Principal determinations

1. Diuretics are not an evidence-based treatment for lipedema itself.
The clearest direct statement is the 2024 German S2k recommendation: do not use diuretics to treat lipedema, while allowing their use when the patient has a separate internal-medicine indication. This was a 94.4% consensus recommendation, not a lipedema diuretic RCT. The 2026 international Delphi paper similarly found no evidence supporting pharmacological treatment of lipedema, but also characterized the underlying evidence as limited. 
AWMF Leitlinienregister
+1

2. “Diuretics always worsen lipedema” is not supported.
No direct lipedema trial or comparative cohort establishing class-specific worsening was verified. The German guideline’s separate-indication exception also contradicts an absolute prohibition. The prudent supported claim is: do not prescribe a diuretic to treat lipedema itself; do not stop a correctly indicated diuretic merely because the person also has lipedema.

3. A separate disease may provide a strong indication.
For heart failure with fluid retention, current AHA/ACC/HFSA guidance recommends diuretics to relieve congestion and prevent worsening; thiazide addition is reserved for inadequate response to moderate- or high-dose loop therapy because of electrolyte risk. In CKD, SGLT2 inhibitors and selected MRAs have kidney or cardiovascular outcome indications rather than merely cosmetic fluid-loss roles. 
professional.heart.org
+2
professional.heart.org
+2

4. Lymphatic and venous swelling require different reasoning.
ISL guidance discourages prolonged systemic diuretic treatment for peripheral lymphedema because benefit is marginal and fluid/electrolyte harm can occur, but it explicitly preserves exceptions for relevant comorbidities, body-cavity effusions and selected complications. Thus, “no diuretic should ever be used in lymphedema” is also too absolute. 
International Society of Lymphology
+1

5. MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors are not merely “water pills.”
Spironolactone, eplerenone and finerenone act through mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade and have disease-specific cardiac or renal roles in defined populations. SGLT2 inhibitors cause some osmotic diuresis, but their guideline-supported reduction of heart-failure and kidney outcomes cannot be explained as water loss alone. Eligibility, renal function, potassium, ketosis risk and other class-specific monitoring remain essential. 
professional.heart.org
+1

6. Swelling after withdrawal is not automatically “rebound.”
The evidence supports at least three possibilities:

transient sodium and water retention after withdrawal in some chronically exposed, carefully selected patients;

recurrence or unmasking of the disease previously controlled, particularly heart failure or hypertension;

persistent edema from another cause, including idiopathic edema that is not attributable to diuretic exposure alone.

Small selected studies therefore cannot justify diagnosing every post-withdrawal increase as rebound or creating a universal taper. Some stable, euvolemic heart-failure patients tolerated withdrawal in a controlled trial, but that result does not apply to active congestion or advanced disease. 
Cardiacos
+3
PubMed Central (PMC)
+3
Europe PMC
+3

7. No lipedema-specific trial of the requested classes was verified.
The documented searches found no candidate randomized or controlled lipedema treatment study involving a loop diuretic, thiazide/thiazide-like drug, MRA or other potassium-sparing drug, acetazolamide, or SGLT2 inhibitor as of 15 August 2026. One current CTIS lipedema study concerns lymphatic-vessel porosity, not diuretic treatment. Because registry APIs, indexing and portal access were imperfect, the conclusion is explicitly “none found in the documented searches,” not proof of nonexistence. The exact queries, candidate records and constraints are in the registry log.

Texto recomendado para una web en español

Los diuréticos no tratan el lipedema en sí. Pueden ser necesarios cuando existe otra indicación bien establecida —por ejemplo, insuficiencia cardíaca con congestión, ascitis por cirrosis, determinados casos de enfermedad renal o hipertensión— y entonces no deben retirarse solo por el diagnóstico de lipedema.

La hinchazón tras reducir o suspender un diurético puede reflejar la reaparición de la enfermedad tratada o, en algunos casos, una retención transitoria de sodio. No debe asumirse automáticamente que sea «rebote».

Los antagonistas del receptor mineralocorticoide y los inhibidores SGLT2 no son simplemente «pastillas para eliminar agua»: algunos reducen eventos cardíacos o renales en poblaciones concretas.

No cambie ni suspenda un diurético sin indicación del equipo tratante. Los cambios requieren valorar síntomas, presión arterial, función renal y electrolitos.

Deliverables

Full audit — PDF

Editable audit — DOCX

Complete delivery package — ZIP

Complete 62-source index — CSV

Audited claim matrix — CSV

Trial-registry search log — CSV

Deduplicated ledger of 67 opened URLs

AEMPS/EMA regulatory extracts

The ZIP also contains the accessibility audit and SHA-256 integrity manifest. Third-party full-text publications are not redistributed in the shareable package; their exact retrieval URLs, PMIDs, DOIs, registry identifiers, dates and access limitations are preserved in the report and source index. No individualized dose, taper or substitution schedule was created.

researcher_responses.overall_summary: Official labels provide disease-specific authorization and safety controls, not lipedema guidance. Lipedema is absent from the inspected EMA/AEMPS-CIMA labels, and no source says diuretics are always harmful in lipedema. Loop, thiazide, and MRA labels concern systemic edema or hypertension; acetazolamide is glaucoma-specific; SGLT2 brands cover diabetes, heart failure, and CKD. All carry important volume, electrolyte, renal, hepatic, or DKA risks and require medical oversight. No inspectable registry record showed a lipedema-specific trial of the requested diuretics.

findings.claim: Official labels do not support diuretic treatment of lipedema
findings.summary: Across the fetched EMA Forxiga and Jardiance documents and nine inspected CIMA fichas técnicas, searches found no lipedema or lipoedema indication. None states that diuretics are always harmful in lipedema. Therefore lipedema use is not label-supported; the absence of wording does not prove universal safety or harm.

findings.claim: Furosemide and torsemide are labeled for systemic edema and hypertension, not lipedema
findings.summary: Furosemide is labeled for edema associated with cardiac, hepatic, renal, and post-burn conditions plus mild or moderate hypertension. Torsemide is labeled for edema associated with cardiac, renal, or hepatic disease and hypertension. Both require supervision and monitoring for volume, electrolytes, renal function, and hepatic complications; these indications do not establish lipedema efficacy.

findings.claim: Indapamide and amiloride-hydrochlorothiazide have narrow labeled uses and substantial electrolyte risks
findings.summary: Indapamide is labeled only for essential hypertension in adults. The inspected Spanish amiloride/hydrochlorothiazide combination is labeled for hypertension and cardiac or cirrhotic edema. Both labels emphasize sodium, potassium, renal, and volume monitoring; the combination adds hyperkalemia, skin-cancer, photosensitivity, and acute-angle-closure warnings. Standalone coverage was limited.

findings.claim: Spironolactone and eplerenone are authorized for specific cardiac, renal, hepatic, or endocrine uses
findings.summary: Spironolactone covers selected heart-failure edema, resistant hypertension, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhotic ascites or edema, and primary hyperaldosteronism. Eplerenone covers selected post-MI LV dysfunction and chronic NYHA II systolic heart failure. Hyperkalemia, renal impairment, RAAS combinations, potassium products, NSAIDs, and other interactions dominate their safety labeling.

findings.claim: Acetazolamide is labeled for glaucoma rather than edema or lipedema
findings.summary: The inspected CIMA acetazolamide record authorizes adjunctive treatment of chronic open-angle or secondary glaucoma and preoperative acute angle-closure glaucoma when local treatment is inadequate. It warns about renal or hepatic disease, sodium or potassium depletion, metabolic acidosis, blood-count abnormalities, and serious hypersensitivity. No edema or lipedema indication appears.

findings.claim: Current EMA SGLT2 indications are diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease
findings.summary: The current EMA Forxiga and Jardiance EPARs authorize dapagliflozin and empagliflozin for type 2 diabetes plus adult symptomatic chronic heart failure and chronic kidney disease; the Forxiga overview includes children from age 10 for diabetes. Labels warn about osmotic diuresis, volume depletion, renal limits, and potentially fatal DKA. None mentions lipedema.

findings.claim: Labels require safety-triggered interruption but do not give general lipedema withdrawal rules
findings.summary: No general taper or abrupt-cessation rule for lipedema was found. Labels instead require temporary or immediate interruption for dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, hyperkalemia, renal deterioration, suspected SGLT2 ketoacidosis, major surgery, or acute illness. Acetazolamide contains a glaucoma-specific gradual-reduction statement, not guidance for lipedema.

findings.claim: No inspectable registry record showed a trial of the requested diuretics specifically for lipedema
findings.summary: The ClinicalTrials.gov lipedema condition query contained no requested diuretic drug names as interventions. NCT03924999 and NCT06549738 used decongestive therapy, compression, exercise, or a pneumatic device, not a diuretic. EUCTR lipedema and lipedema-plus-diuretic queries reported zero matches; WHO results were not parseable, so the negative finding is bounded.

gaps: The Spanish Jardiance EMA PDF was not fetched because the full-response request exceeded the tool limit; the English EMA PDF and Spanish CIMA ficha técnica were used instead.
CIMA did not provide a clean standalone commercial hydrochlorothiazide or amiloride ficha técnica in the inspected results; an amiloride/hydrochlorothiazide combination was used.
CIMA snapshots mark the selected acetazolamide, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin records authorized but not commercial; local stock and later amendments may differ.
A guessed EMA Inspra EPAR URL returned 404; eplerenone was documented from the Spanish CIMA ficha técnica and metadata instead.
WHO ICTRP and ClinicalTrials.gov filtered result pages were JavaScript shells; the inspectable API and EUCTR checks make the negative trial finding bounded, not exhaustive.

researcher_responses.full_research_review:
Scope and method. This audit was retrieved on 15 August 2026 using official EMA EPAR pages and product-information files, Spanish AEMPS/CIMA metadata and full fichas técnicas, and official trial-registry records. Core pages and PDFs were fetched before synthesis and preserved in the evidence directory. The review reports label-supported uses only; it does not infer efficacy for lipedema from an indication for cardiac, renal, hepatic, or other systemic edema. No marketplace, commercial review, or adjacent clinical-guideline claim was used as regulatory evidence.

Source identity and document dates. EMA lists Forxiga as an EU-authorized dapagliflozin product at https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/forxiga. Its English EPAR product-information file is linked at https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/product-information/forxiga-epar-product-information_en.pdf and was marked last updated 12/03/2026; the Spanish product-information PDF was also fetched from https://www.ema.europa.eu/es/documents/product-information/forxiga-epar-product-information_es.pdf. EMA lists Jardiance as an EU-authorized empagliflozin product at https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/jardiance. Its English product-information file at https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/product-information/jardiance-epar-product-information_en.pdf was marked last updated 24/03/2026. The Spanish Jardiance PDF URL was visible on the EMA page but could not be fetched because the response exceeded the content tool limit. The overview-page dates should not be confused with the product-information file dates.

The Spanish representative records were: FUROSEMIDA CINFA 40 mg, CIMA nregistro 64140, ficha técnica dated 15/03/2024, comerc=true; TORASEMIDA CINFA 5/10 mg, nregistro 66315, dated 08/07/2021, comerc=true; AMILORIDA/HIDROCLOROTIAZIDA AUROVITAS 5/50 mg, nregistro 86330, dated 03/02/2023, comerc=true; INDAPAMIDA NORMON 2.5 mg, nregistro 63368, dated 11/03/2022, comerc=true; ESPIRONOLACTONA ACCORD, nregistro 81033, dated 22/05/2025, comerc=true; EPLERENONA VIATRIS, nregistro 78657, dated 28/01/2023, comerc=true; ACETAZOLAMIDA ASPIRE, nregistro 91497, dated 29/07/2026, comerc=false; DAPAGLIFLOZINA AUROVITAS, nregistro 89963, dated 22/10/2025, comerc=false; and EMPAGLIFLOZINA KERN PHARMA, nregistro 91044, dated 26/02/2026, comerc=false. The CIMA commerc field is a snapshot of the Spanish record and should not be treated as a universal statement about authorization or availability.

Loop diuretics. Furosemide CIMA FT 64140, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/64140/FT_64140.html, authorizes treatment of edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis including ascites, renal disease including nephrotic syndrome, and post-burn edema, and also mild or moderate hypertension. Contraindications include hypersensitivity, possible sulfonamide cross-sensitivity, hypovolemia or dehydration, anuric renal failure not responding to treatment, severe hypokalemia, severe hyponatremia, hepatic precoma or coma with encephalopathy, and breastfeeding. Warnings require regular medical supervision, attention to urinary obstruction, and periodic serum sodium, potassium, and creatinine checks. Dehydration, hypovolemia, electrolyte or acid-base abnormalities should be corrected and may require temporary interruption. Renal and hepatic disease, hypotension, and hypoproteinemia require caution. Important interactions include aminoglycosides and cisplatin with ototoxic or nephrotoxic risk, lithium toxicity, sucralfate reducing absorption, antihypertensives and RAAS drugs increasing hypotension or renal risk, and NSAIDs reducing effect and increasing acute-kidney-injury risk in volume-depleted patients. The FT did not give a general taper or abrupt-cessation rule.

Torasemide CIMA FT 66315, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/66315/FT_66315.html, authorizes edema associated with congestive heart failure, renal or hepatic disease, and treatment of hypertension alone or with other antihypertensives. Contraindications are hypersensitivity to torasemide, sulfonylureas, or excipients, anuria with renal failure, and hepatic coma until improvement or correction. The FT warns that profound diuresis can deplete water and electrolytes and requires careful medical supervision. It calls for monitoring of blood electrolyte balance, potassium, glucose, uric acid, and creatinine, particularly in long-term treatment and older adults; urinary retention must be corrected or closely monitored. Cirrhotic ascites should be initiated in hospital because overly rapid diuresis can precipitate severe electrolyte changes or hepatic coma. Interactions include potassium-depletion-related cardiac-glycoside toxicity, corticosteroids or laxatives, aminoglycosides and platinum drugs, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, lithium, cholestyramine, probenecid, and CYP2C8/CYP2C9 substrate interactions. No general withdrawal instruction was found.

Thiazide/thiazide-like agents and amiloride. The CIMA indapamide FT 63368, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/63368/FT_63368.html, lists only essential hypertension in adults. Contraindications are sulfonamide hypersensitivity, severe renal failure, hepatic encephalopathy or severe hepatic dysfunction, and hypokalemia. It warns that thiazides may precipitate hepatic encephalopathy and says treatment should be interrupted immediately if that occurs; photosensitivity reactions also warrant interruption. Sodium should be checked before and regularly during treatment, with closer monitoring in older adults and cirrhosis. Potassium depletion is a major risk; the FT also calls for monitoring magnesium, calcium, glucose, uric acid, and renal function, and warns that renal hypovolemia can raise urea and creatinine. Interactions include lithium, high-dose NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors in sodium-depleted patients, other potassium-losing agents, metformin when renal function declines, ciclosporin or tacrolimus, and corticosteroids. It also contains a condition-specific instruction to stop before parathyroid evaluation, not a lipedema cessation rule.

Because the inspected CIMA amiloride search did not yield a clean standalone commercial record, the primary source used was AMILORIDA/HIDROCLOROTIAZIDA AUROVITAS nregistro 86330, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/86330/FT_86330.html. It is labeled for adult hypertension, cardiac edema, and edema associated with hepatic cirrhosis including ascites; the amiloride component is described as useful where excess potassium loss is anticipated or potassium balance is important. Contraindications include hyperkalemia above 5.5 mEq/L, other potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium supplements, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, anuria or severe progressive renal disease, inability to monitor urea and electrolytes, diabetic nephropathy, severe hepatic failure or cirrhotic precoma, and Addison disease. The FT emphasizes clinical, laboratory, and ECG monitoring because hyperkalemia can be fatal, especially in older adults and patients with cirrhosis, cardiac edema, or renal involvement. It says to stop immediately for hyperkalemia and to stop the diuretic if azotemia is accompanied by oliguria. Sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium, renal function, glucose, skin reactions, photosensitivity, and acute-angle-closure eye symptoms are relevant monitoring domains. Interactions include lithium, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, trilostane, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, potassium products, and antidiabetics. This combination source does not establish the authorization or availability of standalone hydrochlorothiazide or amiloride.

Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists. Spironolactone CIMA FT 81033, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/81033/FT_81033.html, authorizes treatment of edema in congestive heart failure, severe heart failure including NYHA III-IV settings, resistant hypertension as adjunctive therapy, nephrotic syndrome, hepatic cirrhosis with ascites or edema, and diagnosis or treatment of primary hyperaldosteronism. Contraindications include severe renal impairment, hyponatremia, Addison disease, baseline hyperkalemia above 5.0, potassium-sparing diuretics including eplerenone, potassium supplements, and dual ACE-inhibitor plus ARB blockade. The label warns of hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and transient BUN elevation and requires regular fluid and electrolyte supervision, especially in older adults and renal or hepatic disease. In severe heart failure it specifies serial potassium and creatinine monitoring and interruption for specified high potassium or creatinine values. Interactions include potassium supplements and salt substitutes, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, NSAIDs, aldosterone blockers, heparin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciclosporin, and antihypertensives or cardiac glycosides. No general taper instruction was found.

Eplerenone CIMA FT 78657, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/78657/FT_78657.html, authorizes add-on treatment after myocardial infarction in stable adults with LV systolic dysfunction and clinical heart-failure signs, and add-on treatment in adults with chronic NYHA II systolic LV dysfunction. Contraindications include baseline potassium above 5.0, severe renal impairment with eGFR below 30, severe hepatic impairment Child-Pugh C, potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium supplements, potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, and triple ACE-inhibitor plus ARB plus eplerenone therapy. Potassium should be checked before treatment, during the early period after initiation or dose change, and periodically; renal function and electrolytes require monitoring. The label provides suspension and medically monitored restart conditions for high potassium, not a taper regimen. Interactions include RAAS blockers, NSAIDs, lithium, trimethoprim, ciclosporin or tacrolimus, potent CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers, and potassium products. The guessed EMA Inspra page https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/Inspra and a guessed direct EMA product-information PDF returned 404, so this agent is documented through CIMA.

Acetazolamide. CIMA FT 91497, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/91497/FT_91497.html, authorizes adjunctive treatment of chronic simple or open-angle glaucoma, secondary glaucoma, and preoperative acute angle-closure glaucoma when local therapy is insufficient. Contraindications include sulfonamide hypersensitivity, severe hepatic disease or cirrhosis because of encephalopathy risk, severe renal failure, sodium or potassium depletion, Addison disease, hyperchloremic acidosis, cor pulmonale, and prolonged treatment of certain non-congestive angle-closure glaucoma. The FT calls for blood-count monitoring before and during long-term treatment, regular serum electrolytes, and renal and hepatic-function tests. It warns about hypokalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis, gout, severe sulfonamide reactions, acute myopia or secondary angle closure, choroidal effusion, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema; these events require interruption or suspension as specified. Interactions include salicylates, other carbonic-anhydrase inhibitors, thiazides and other diuretics, corticosteroids, amphotericin B, anticonvulsants, sodium bicarbonate, and antidiabetic agents. The FT contains a glaucoma-specific statement about gradual reduction in the acute-glaucoma regimen, but this is not guidance for lipedema or general diuretic withdrawal.

SGLT2 inhibitors. The current Forxiga EMA overview states that dapagliflozin is used for inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes in adults and children from age 10 with diet and exercise, as monotherapy when metformin is inappropriate or as add-on therapy, and for symptomatic chronic heart failure and chronic kidney disease in adults. The current Jardiance EMA overview states adult type 2 diabetes, symptomatic chronic heart failure, and chronic kidney disease indications. The Spanish CIMA dapagliflozin generic FT 89963, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/89963/FT_89963.html, has a product-specific section 4.1 that shows type 2 diabetes; its CIMA record was not commercial in the retrieved snapshot. The CIMA empagliflozin FT 91044, https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/91044/FT_91044.html, records diabetes, heart-failure, and chronic-kidney-disease indications; its CIMA record was also not commercial in the snapshot. Product-specific generic wording should therefore not be substituted for the current originator EPAR without checking the exact product.

Dapagliflozin labeling warns that renal glucose-lowering efficacy declines with impaired renal function and that initiation is not recommended below the stated renal threshold in the FT; severe hepatic impairment increases exposure. Because it increases diuresis, the label calls for monitoring volume status, blood pressure, hematocrit, electrolytes, and renal function, with temporary interruption until volume depletion is corrected. Rare, potentially fatal DKA requires immediate interruption when suspected or diagnosed, interruption for major surgery or acute severe illness, ketone monitoring, and no routine restart after DKA unless another precipitating cause is identified and resolved. Fournier gangrene, urinary infection, and hypoglycemia with insulin or secretagogues are additional warnings. Thiazide or loop diuretics can increase dehydration and hypotension risk; lithium levels may change and require monitoring; insulin and secretagogues increase hypoglycemia risk; and metabolic or transporter interactions are product-specific.

Empagliflozin labeling similarly warns that osmotic diuresis can cause hypotension or volume depletion and calls for renal-function, volume, blood-pressure, hematocrit, and electrolyte monitoring. The FT limits initiation at very low eGFR, states that glucose-lowering efficacy falls with renal impairment, and advises caution or limited use in severe hepatic disease. DKA can be fatal or potentially fatal; treatment should be interrupted immediately for suspected or confirmed DKA and during major surgery or acute serious illness, with resumption only after clinical and ketone stability. The label notes that DKA can persist after stopping and advises against restarting after DKA unless another cause is found and corrected. Loops or thiazides add volume-depletion and hypotension risk; insulin or sulfonylureas add hypoglycemia risk; lithium levels may change; and UGT or other metabolic interactions are product-specific.

Lipedema and always-harmful wording check. Regex searches across the preserved CIMA and EMA label/page text found no lipedema or lipoedema mention. No inspected regulatory source says that diuretics are always harmful, always dangerous, or always contraindicated in lipedema. This is an absence finding limited to the inspected official sources. It does not establish benefit, safety, or harm for lipedema and does not convert off-label practice into an authorized indication.

Discontinuation and medical-supervision synthesis. The labels consistently use medical-supervision language rather than a general class-wide taper rule. Furosemide and torsemide require supervised correction of volume or electrolyte problems; the amiloride combination requires immediate stopping for hyperkalemia and stopping for certain renal deterioration; indapamide requires interruption for hepatic encephalopathy or photosensitivity; spironolactone and eplerenone specify potassium- or renal-triggered interruption; acetazolamide specifies interruption for serious hematologic, hypersensitivity, ocular, metabolic, or pulmonary events; and SGLT2 labels specify immediate or temporary interruption for DKA, severe illness, surgery, or volume depletion. None gives lipedema-specific cessation advice. The acetazolamide gradual-reduction wording is confined to acute glaucoma management and should not be generalized.

Registry audit. The inspectable ClinicalTrials.gov v2 query https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.cond=Lipedema&pageSize=100 was screened for furosemide, torsemide or torasemide, spironolactone, eplerenone, hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide, amiloride, acetazolamide, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin; none appeared as a requested diuretic intervention. NCT03924999, https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT03924999, was a completed study of complete decongestive therapy, manual lymphatic drainage, compression, and exercise versus intermittent pneumatic compression and exercise, not a drug trial. NCT06549738, https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06549738, was a completed study of a pneumatic compression device and compression leggings, not a diuretic trial. A broad registry description contains incidental diuretic-related wording in an edema discussion, but not a diuretic intervention. EU Clinical Trials Register queries https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/search?query=lipedema and https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/search?query=lipedema+diuretic both rendered zero matching trials. The WHO ICTRP page https://trialsearch.who.int/?query=lipedema was fetched, but its result area was JavaScript-rendered and did not yield inspectable records; it was not used to claim a definitive negative.

Interpretation. Any use of these medicines for lipedema alone would be off-label relative to the inspected product information unless a separate product-specific authorization is established. Labels for systemic edema, hypertension, glaucoma, diabetes, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease should not be read as clinical guidance for lipedema, and the label safety warnings should not be converted into an efficacy or harm conclusion about lipedema.

Resumen breve de seguridad en español, sin dosis ni instrucciones de retirada: Los prospectos revisados no autorizan estos fármacos para el lipedema. Pueden causar deshidratación, bajadas de tensión y alteraciones de sodio o potasio; los ahorradores de potasio pueden causar hiperpotasemia y los inhibidores SGLT2 cetoacidosis. Requieren indicación y vigilancia médica, especialmente con enfermedad renal o hepática o combinaciones de medicamentos. No iniciar, suspender ni combinar por cuenta propia; ante síntomas graves, buscar atención urgente.
